How to Choose a Chinese Brand Name That Actually Passes CNIPA Examination

Foreign brands often choose a Chinese name for marketing reasons and only then ask whether it can be registered. That order is backwards. In a first-to-file system, the cheaper and safer sequence is to clear the name first and fall in love with it second.

Your Chinese Name Is a Separate Right

A foreign brand entering China usually has a Latin mark and, sooner or later, a Chinese name. Legally these are two different rights. Registering the Latin word does not protect a Chinese-character version, and a Chinese name adopted by consumers is not automatically yours to enforce. The safer sequence is to test registrability first and choose the name second, rather than fall in love with a name, print packaging, and only then discover a blocking citation.

This matters because the market will produce a Chinese name whether you plan one or not. Consumers and retailers shorten, transliterate or translate foreign brands into everyday nicknames, and those nicknames are exactly what a squatter monitors. A name built purely for marketing, with a pleasant sound, an auspicious meaning and elegant characters, can still fail examination if it is descriptive, generic, or too close to an earlier filing along any of the three axes described below.

Treat the exercise as a legal availability question with a marketing input, not the reverse. Agree a shortlist of candidates, clear each one, and only then commission artwork and launch materials. The cost of dropping a candidate at shortlist stage is trivial compared with rebranding after a refusal.

The Three Axes of Similarity: Sound, Form and Meaning

CNIPA examines similarity between Chinese-character marks along three axes, and a conflict on any one of them can be enough to refuse an application. Understanding them is what turns a name from something that sounds nice into something likely to survive examination.

AxisWhat the examiner comparesPractical check
SoundStandard Mandarin pronunciation and pinyin, including tone patterns and homophonesRead candidates aloud; list same-syllable and near-syllable alternatives
FormThe structure and arrangement of the Chinese characters, radicals and stroke compositionCompare visual similarity character by character, not just the overall impression
MeaningThe sense of the characters and correspondence with the foreign mark or its translationCheck literal meaning, translated equivalents and connotations in context

A candidate can be clear on one axis and blocked on another: a name that reads differently but shares a distinctive character, or one that looks different but conveys the same meaning as an earlier mark. Clearance therefore has to run all three comparisons against the register, not just a search for identical characters.

Absolute Grounds: Articles 15, 17 and 19

Beyond conflicts with earlier rights, a name must be registrable in its own right. Article 17 refuses signs that are generic names of the goods, merely descriptive of their characteristics, or otherwise lacking distinctive character, with the important exception that a sign may become registrable where distinctiveness has been acquired through use. A name that simply states what the product is, praises its quality, or names a place or ingredient will struggle, and the exception requires a real evidence file of genuine use.

Article 15 sets out prohibited signs that cannot be used or registered as trademarks, and Article 19 targets bad-faith applications: a filing made with no intention to use and clearly exceeding normal business needs may be refused. For a brand owner, the practical point is the mirror image. Choose a coined, distinctive name, keep records showing an intention to use it, and avoid a portfolio of speculative defensive filings that looks like hoarding.

Coined beats descriptive. Invented combinations of characters with no direct dictionary meaning are usually easier to clear and easier to defend than a literal translation of your slogan or product category. They also give you a cleaner story when arguing acquired distinctiveness later.

A Six-Lane Clearance Search

A clearance search for a Chinese name has to cover six lanes. Search the Chinese characters themselves; the pinyin and its homophones; the Latin or English source word; translated equivalents of the meaning; dialect and regional phonetic variants that produce awkward or similar readings; and the colloquial names consumers have already coined for your brand. Missing the last lane is a common reason a launch-name search looks clean while the market is already using a variant a squatter can register.

Use the official database as one input, not as a verdict. The publicly searchable register is not real time: there is a period during which recently filed applications are not yet visible, and the data may lag. A search result is therefore a risk assessment, not a guarantee of registrability. Do not treat a no-hits result as clearance to print packaging, and do not assume a fixed blind-spot duration; check the current position with your agent rather than relying on a stated number of months.

A no-hits result does not mean registrable. Combine an official-database search with a broader commercial search, keep dated records of what was searched and when, and refresh the search immediately before filing. Where a candidate is marginal, have a second and third choice cleared at the same time.

File the Word and the Device Separately

Examination looks at a combined mark element by element. When a device and a word are filed together, each component is assessed, and a problem with one element can hold up the whole application. The usual recommendation is to file the Chinese-character word mark, the Latin word mark and the device as separate applications: each stands or falls on its own, each is a separate right, and a refusal or opposition against one does not freeze the others.

File the English and Chinese versions together as a matter of portfolio design, not as a single composite. They protect different things and support different enforcement and use-evidence files. If the chosen name is weak on distinctiveness, plan from the start for the evidence that Article 17's acquired-distinctiveness exception requires: dated advertising, sales and marketplace records showing that consumers recognise the name as yours.

Finally, register in the classes you use and keep the Latin and Chinese names consistent across packaging, platform listings and company materials. Inconsistent use creates the nicknames that make a later clearance search harder. Sources and Caveats

Basis: Articles 15, 17, 19 and 20 of the Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) (adopted 26 June 2026, effective 1 January 2027); general CNIPA examination practice on the sound, form and meaning of Chinese-character marks and on the examination of combined marks; practitioner guidance on Chinese brand naming. Official database coverage and examination standards may change, so confirm the current position and the live register against the official announcements and rules before filing. This is general information, not legal advice.
